endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: For example, mammograms with higher risk scores can be prioritized for interpretation ahead of mammograms with lower risk scores.

endorsements.title: Adoption of AI in Healthcare Delivery Systems: Early Applications and Impacts
endorsements.quote: Predict and prevent denials by addressing issues prior to claims submissions;

endorsements.title: Choosing the right artificial intelligence solutions for your radiology department: key factors to consider
endorsements.quote: Such a solution should immediately distinguish pathological cases from normal ones with binary classification, ideally identify priority cases with acute findings, and highlight them on the radiologist\u2019s worklist for triage.

evidence.title: Cost-effectiveness of immediate prioritisation of chest X-rays using artificial intelligence in lung cancer in England: the LungIMPACT study
evidence.outcome: Time from CXR to lung cancer diagnosis; cost-effectiveness of AI worklist prioritisation
evidence.effect: AI prioritisation did not reduce time to diagnosis and was not cost-effective vs AI without prioritisation; budget impact £2 million per year in England.
evidence.quote: The LungIMPACT randomised study found that the use of an artificial intelligence (AI) tool to flag and prioritise chest X-rays (CXR) referred from primary care in the human reporter’s worklist, did not reduce time from CXR to lung cancer (LC) diagnosis.

evidence.title: Triaging mammography with artificial intelligence: an implementation study
evidence.outcome: Time to additional imaging and biopsy diagnosis with AI prioritization vs standard
evidence.effect: Mean time to additional imaging fell 25% (25.6 to 19.1 days, p<0.001); time to biopsy fell 30% (55.9 to 39.2 days, p=0.003); all 6 cancers AI-prioritized.
evidence.quote: In comparison, mean T A in the experimental group was reduced by 25% to 19.1 days (ΔT A =−6.4 days, upper limit of one-sided 95% CI = −0.3, p <0.001), while the mean T B was reduced by 30% to 39.2 days (ΔT B =−16.8 days, upper limit of one-sided 95% CI = −5.1, p =0.003).

evidence.title: Improving In-person Interpreter Utilization in Complex Care: Findings from a Stepped-Wedge Cluster Randomized Trial of Integrated Artificial Intelligence
evidence.outcome: Time from study entry to first in-person interpreter visit, intervention vs control
evidence.effect: Time to receiving interpreter did not differ between groups (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.81-1.29, p=0.87); the abstract reports an OR and CI close to >1 for receiving an interpreter.
evidence.quote: Time to receiving interpreter did not differ between groups (HR = 1.02, 95% C.I. (0.81, 1.29), p = 0.87).

evidence.title: AI-based chest X-ray prioritization in the lung cancer diagnostic pathway: the LungIMPACT randomized controlled trial
evidence.outcome: Time to CT and lung cancer diagnosis with vs without AI worklist prioritization
evidence.effect: Median time to CT 53 vs 53 days (ratio of geometric means 0.97, 95% CI 0.93-1.02; P=0.31); time to diagnosis 44 vs 46 days (ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.83-1.16; P=0.84); no stage difference (P=0.34).
evidence.quote: AI prioritization of CXR requested by UK primary care has no significant impact on the lung cancer pathway.

evidence.title: Real-World Impact of an AI-Driven Teleradiology Workflow for Intracranial Hemorrhage Detection: Reducing Diagnostic Delays Across a Multicenter Emergency Network
evidence.outcome: PACS-to-assessment time and report turnaround time before vs after AI triage prioritization
evidence.effect: Mean PTAT reduced by 13.72 min (p=0.002) and RTAT by 26.62 min (p=0.001); overnight reduction of 26 min (p=0.001); ICH-positive PTAT drop of 31.43 min not significant.
evidence.quote: Integrating an AI-driven tool for the detection of ICH into a teleradiology workflow significantly reduced PTAT and RTAT without compromising diagnostic accuracy.

evidence.title: Towards clinical implementation of an AI-algorithm for detection of cervical spine fractures on computed tomography
evidence.outcome: Time between CT acquisition and first opening of the scan
evidence.effect: DNT was 18 % (5 min) shorter overall and 46 % (16 min) shorter for fracture-positive scans in the prospective cohort.
evidence.quote: In scans positive for cervical spine fracture according to the reference standard, DNT was 46 % (16 min) shorter in the prospective cohort.

evidence.title: Prospective Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Triage of Incidental Pulmonary Emboli on Contrast-Enhanced CT Examinations of the Chest or Abdomen
evidence.outcome: Report turnaround time and sensitivity with vs without AI triage notification
evidence.effect: Sensitivity rose from 80.0% without AI to 96.2% with AI (p = .03), specificity unchanged at 99.9%. Mean turnaround for IPE-positive exams did not differ significantly: 78.3 vs 74.6 minutes (p = .26).
evidence.quote: The mean report turnaround time for IPE-positive examinations was not significantly different between radiologists without AI and radiologists with AI (78.3 vs 74.6 minutes, p = .26).

evidence.title: Development and evaluation of an artificial intelligence-based workflow for the prioritization of patient portal messages
evidence.outcome: Time high-scoring patient messages sit unread, pre-post difference-in-difference
evidence.effect: Improvement beyond trend of 21 minutes in time high-scoring messages sit unread (63 vs 42 minutes for messages sent outside business hours).
evidence.quote: In a pre-post analysis (n = 396 466), an improvement exceeding the trend was observed in the time high-scoring messages sit unread (21 minutes, 63 vs 42 for messages sent outside business hours).

evidence.title: Prospective Evaluation of Artificial Intelligence Triage of Intracranial Hemorrhage on Noncontrast Head CT Examinations
evidence.outcome: Report turnaround time for ICH-positive exams with AI triage notification
evidence.effect: Mean report turnaround time 147.1 minutes without AI vs 149.9 minutes with AI (p = .11); no improvement.
evidence.quote: An AI triage system for ICH detection did not improve radiologists' diagnostic performance or report turnaround times.

evidence.title: Real-World Performance of Pneumothorax-Detecting Artificial Intelligence Algorithm and its Impact on Radiologist Reporting Times
evidence.outcome: Radiologist report turnaround time for confirmed pneumothorax CXRs with vs without AI alerts
evidence.effect: Median reporting time reduced by 46% with AI integration (100 vs. 186 min, p < .001)
evidence.quote: Median reporting time in CXRs with radiologist-confirmed PTx was reduced by 46% in those with AI integration as compared to those without AI integration (100 vs. 186 min, p < .001).

evidence.title: Guiding Clostridioides difficile Infection Prevention Efforts in a Hospital Setting With AI
evidence.outcome: Pharmacist engagement with AI high-risk flag in existing review dashboard
evidence.effect: Flag used to sort pharmacist medication review queue; 6 of 7 pharmacists found workflow not disruptive, all 7 contacted care teams; piperacillin-tazobactam relative reduction 16.8% in high-risk alerted patients.
evidence.quote: However, of the 7 pharmacists interviewed, 6 indicated the new workflow was not disruptive, and all 7 contacted the patients’ care team based on the alerts (eTables 7 and 8 in Supplement 1 ).

evidence.title: Impact of a computed tomography-based artificial intelligence software on radiologists' workflow for detecting acute intracranial hemorrhage
evidence.outcome: Reading order and early diagnosis rate of AIH cases before vs after AI prioritization
evidence.effect: Early diagnosis rate rose from 0.49 to 0.76 (P=0.013); median reading order of AIH cases fell from 7.25 to 1.5 (P<0.001); Kendall's Tau fell from 0.61 to 0.01.
evidence.quote: Additionally, the early diagnosis rate significantly increased [from 0.49 (0.34-0.63) to 0.76 (0.60-0.93), P = 0.013], and the daily median reading order of AIH cases significantly decreased [from 7.25 (Q1-Q3: 3-10.75) to 1.5 (1-3), P < 0.001] after the implementation.

evidence.title: AI triage of duodenal biopsies improves workflow
evidence.outcome: Reporting turnaround time with AI-prioritised queue vs routine pathway
evidence.effect: Coeliac disease reported in 6 vs 10 days; non-neoplastic abnormalities 7 vs 10 days (both p<0.005); neoplastic lesions not reported quicker.
evidence.quote: In the AI triage workstream coeliac disease, and non-neoplastic abnormalities as a group, were reported quicker than in the standard workstream (6 days vs 10 days and 7 days vs 10 days, respectively, both p<0.005), but neoplastic lesions were not reported quicker.

evidence.title: Prospective deployment of AI-based risk stratification to enable expedited mammography workflow in a safety-net setting
evidence.outcome: Time to screening results, diagnostic evaluation, and biopsy for AI-prioritized patients
evidence.effect: Expedited (AI top-10% risk) patients vs controls with screen-detected cancers: reductions of 99.1%, 99.1%, and 87.2% in time to screening results, diagnostic evaluation, and biopsy
evidence.quote: Time to screening results, diagnostic evaluation, and biopsy were significantly shorter in expedited patients versus control patients with screen-detected cancers, with reductions of 99.1%, 99.1%, and 87.2%, respectively.

evidence.title: Radiologist Worklist Reprioritization Using Artificial Intelligence: Impact on Report Turnaround Times for CTPA Examinations Positive for Acute Pulmonary Embolism
evidence.outcome: Report turnaround, wait, and read times for PE-positive CTPA exams
evidence.effect: Post-AI vs pre-AI: turnaround 47.6 vs 59.9 min (diff 12.3, 95% CI 0.6-26.0); wait 21.4 vs 33.4 min (diff 12.0); read time no difference (26.3 vs 26.5 min).
evidence.quote: For PE-positive examinations, the post-AI period, compared with the pre-AI period, had significantly shorter mean report turnaround time (47.6 vs 59.9 minutes; mean difference, 12.3 minutes [95% CI, 0.6-26.0 minutes]) and mean wait time (21.4 vs 33.4 minutes; mean difference, 12.0 minutes [95% CI, 0.9-25.3 minutes]) but no significant difference in mean read time (26.3 vs 26.5 minutes; mean difference, 0.2 minutes [95% CI, -2.8 to 3.2 minutes]).

evidence.title: Natural language processing system for rapid detection and intervention of mental health crisis chat messages
evidence.outcome: Median time from message receipt to crisis specialist triage before vs after deployment
evidence.effect: Daily median time to crisis specialist triage was 8 to 13 min after deployment, compared to 9 h before deployment.
evidence.quote: The daily median time from message receipt to crisis specialist triage ranges from 8 to 13 min, compared to 9 h before the deployment of the system.

evidence.title: Use of a Deep Learning Algorithm for Detection and Triage of Cancer-associated Incidental Pulmonary Embolism
evidence.outcome: Report turnaround time and time to treatment before vs after AI detection and triage
evidence.effect: Median report turnaround 0.66 h vs 24.68 h; time to treatment 0.98 h vs 28.05 h (both P < .001); reported iPE prevalence 2.5% vs 0.8%.
evidence.quote: In conclusion, the use of AI for detection and triage of iPE in clinical practice resulted in an increased detection rate of iPE and significantly shorter report turnaround time and time to treatment for patients with cancer-associated iPE.

evidence.title: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Triage on Radiologist Report Turnaround Time: Real-World Time Savings and Insights From Model Predictions
evidence.venue: Journal of the American College of Radiology : JACR
evidence.outcome: Report turnaround time for PE-positive CTPA exams before vs after AI worklist prioritization
evidence.effect: Work-hour time savings 22.2 min (95% CI 5.85-38.6), significant (P=.004). Off-hour savings 2.82 min (-11.1 to 16.7), not significant (P=.345).
evidence.quote: Clinically observed time savings during work hours (22.2 [95% confidence interval: 5.85-38.6] min) were significant (P = .004), while off-hour (2.82 [-11.1 to 16.7] min) were not (P = .345).

evidence.title: Impact of an AI-powered hospital admission prediction dashboard to guide medication reconciliation in the emergency department: a retrospective before-after study
evidence.outcome: Proportion of ED patients with correct and potentially unnecessary medication reconciliation before vs after admission-prediction prioritization dashboard
evidence.effect: Correct MR rose from 86.4% to 89.0% (p = 0.0002); potentially unnecessary MR fell from 17.9% to 12.6% (p < 0.0001).
evidence.quote: After implementing the dashboard, the proportion of patients with correct MR increased from 86.4 to 89.0% (p = 0.0002), and the proportion of patients with potentially unnecessary MR decreased from 17.9 to 12.6% (p < 0.0001).

evidence.title: Does Splitting a Triage Decision Across Agents Hide Bias or Help Catch It? A Multi-Agent Simulation Study of LLM-Based Resource Allocation Under Audit Capacity Constraints
evidence.outcome: Audit coverage under capacity constraint with risk-ordered queue vs first-come-first-served
evidence.effect: Risk-ordered audit queue raised coverage from 65.6% to 91.7% (p = 0.028) under the same capacity constraint.
evidence.quote: A follow-up experiment shows that reordering the audit queue by estimated risk, rather than first-come-first-served, recovers most of the lost coverage under the same capacity constraint (65.6% to 91.7%, p = 0.028).

evidence.title: A Deep Learning Framework for Automated Triage of Breast Cancer Biopsies in Malaysia: A Pragmatic Trial to Reduce Resource Consumption and Diagnostic Turnaround Time
evidence.outcome: Suspicious-case diagnostic turnaround time
evidence.effect: Average TAT for suspicious cases reduced 38.2%, from 7.2 to 4.5 days; benign TAT slightly increased.
evidence.quote: The simulation demonstrated that the triage system reduced the average TAT for suspicious cases by 38.2% (from 7.2 to 4.5 days) while slightly increasing the TAT for benign cases.

evidence.title: Continuous predicted risks should be retained when deploying clinical prediction models
evidence.outcome: PPV, sensitivity, mean rank of true positives when ranking by predicted risk versus risk groups under resource constraints
evidence.effect: Ranking patients by predicted probabilities gave better performance than risk groups alone; benefits grew with discrimination and prevalence and were greatest when resource constraints were highest.
evidence.quote: Using predicted probabilities to rank patients by predicted risk led to model performance benefits when compared to risk groups alone.

evidence.title: AI-Powered Chest X-Ray for Diagnosing Pulmonary Tuberculosis in County and Township Health Care Facilities in Yichang: Retrospective, Real-World Study
evidence.outcome: AI score quartiles for prioritizing radiologist review of high-risk patients
evidence.effect: Scores >0.75 (34.2% of CAD-positive) contained 189/229 (82.5%) of confirmed PTB cases; P for trend <.001.
evidence.quote: Most confirmed patients (189/229, 82.5%) had CAD scores exceeding the 75% quantiles (Q75) threshold, which accounted for 34.2% (4618/13,515) of all CAD-positive patients ( Table 3 ).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-powered tiered early warning framework addressing high false alarm rates for in-hospital mortality prediction
evidence.outcome: Mortality rate across risk-tiered subgroups to prioritize response
evidence.effect: Upper-intermediate subgroup mortality 20.14% vs 7.64% (intermediate) and 3.22% (lower-intermediate), enabling graded clinical response.
evidence.quote: Notably, the M+ subgroup had a markedly higher mortality rate (20.14%) compared to M (7.64%) and M- (3.22%), indicating meaningful risk stratification within the intermediate zone.

evidence.title: Revenue-sensitive evaluation of AI-assisted ICD-10-CM coding and human-AI collaboration under dual DRG payment systems
evidence.outcome: CRS reduction from human review queue prioritized by revenue risk versus random or confidence-based prioritization
evidence.effect: At 20% review rate, revenue-targeted prioritization achieved 43.2% CRS reduction vs 20.0% random and 19.7% confidence-based; 91% of oracle bound (47.4%). Simulation assumed perfect correction.
evidence.quote: At the practically relevant 20% review rate: S3 achieved F1-micro of 0.7423 with 43.2% CRS reduction; S3-TW (Tw-DRG targeting) achieved similar F1 of 0.7435 with 43.1% CRS reduction; while S2 (confidence-based) achieved only 19.7% and S1 (random) achieved 20.0% CRS reduction.

evidence.title: Simulation of AI-driven CT Queue Prioritization in the Emergency Department
evidence.outcome: Wait times for actionable vs nonactionable CT studies under AI prioritization vs first-in-first-out
evidence.effect: Median wait for actionable studies reduced by 10.75 min; 90th percentile by 43.36 min; actionable findings within 1 hour rose from 48.33% to 57.30%; nonactionable 90th percentile wait increased 14.46 min.
evidence.quote: Compared with the first-in, first-out policy, the AI-based dispatch policy reduced median wait times for actionable studies in the internal test set (7637 of 20 795 [36.73%]) by 10.75 minutes (95% CI: -12.40, -9.10) and 90th-percentile wait times by 43.36 minutes (95% CI: -50.58, -36.80).

evidence.title: Cross-model disagreement as a reference-free signal for prioritizing human review in medical speech transcription
evidence.outcome: Review workload to recover errors
evidence.effect: Flagging A ≤ 6 selected 28.6% of positions and captured 93.7% of HC errors.
evidence.quote: Flagging tokens with A ≤ 6 selected 28.6% of positions and captured 93.7% of HC errors ( Figure 6B ).

commentary.bottom_line: Across 25 studies, AI-ordered queues usually shortened waits for flagged items in imaging, pathology, patient messages, and crisis chat, but the three randomized trials found benefit, no difference, and a lack of cost-effectiveness. Deployers may expect faster handling of flagged items, while evidence that this improves patient outcomes without delaying lower-priority items remains limited.

perspectives.view: Three randomized trials disagree. A United States trial cut mean time to biopsy by 30% (55.9 to 39.2 days). An English trial found no reduction in time to lung cancer diagnosis, and an interpreter trial found no difference (HR 1.02). Most other studies are nonrandomized or simulated and measure turnaround time, so inconsistency and indirect outcomes lower certainty.

Effects varied by time of day and setting. One pulmonary embolism study saved 22.2 minutes during work hours but 2.82 minutes off hours, which was not significant. An intracranial hemorrhage study found no turnaround gain (147.1 vs 149.9 minutes). In a pharmacy deployment, 6 of 7 pharmacists found the sorted queue not disruptive.

The only trial in limited English proficiency patients prioritized inpatients for interpreter visits and found no difference in time to an interpreter (HR 1.02, 95% CI 0.81-1.29). A replay study using rural Chinese data found that scores above 0.75 held 82.5% of confirmed tuberculosis cases, but that study did not test live routing.

An English trial estimated a £2 million annual budget impact and found prioritization not cost-effective compared with AI used without prioritization. In a before-after study, admission-prediction targeting cut potentially unnecessary medication reconciliations from 17.9% to 12.6%. A revenue-review simulation reached a 43.2% reduction versus 20.0% for random review, and it assumed perfect correction.

Score-based ordering shortened waits for patients who reached out. High-scoring portal messages sat unread 21 minutes less beyond trend. Median time to a crisis specialist fell from 9 hours to 8 to 13 minutes after a chat triage model was deployed. Neither study reported whether lower-scored patients waited longer to reach a human.

commentary.research_gap: Outside imaging, one randomized trial tested live score-based ordering, for interpreter visits, and it found no difference in time to an interpreter. Score-based ordering of claims, coding, revenue, and audit review was tested only in simulation, and portal message and crisis chat triage were tested only in nonrandomized designs. Few studies measured patient outcomes such as time to treatment, harm, or missed diagnoses, few reported waits for lower-priority items alongside flagged ones, and only one study reported costs.
commentary.underserved_note: One cluster randomized trial enrolled limited English proficiency inpatients and found no difference in time to an interpreter, and one offline study used rural Chinese data. No test reported including Medicaid, safety-net, or low-literacy populations. Deployers serving these groups therefore cannot assume that the reported time savings apply, and they may need to check whether score-based ordering moves their patients lower in the queue.
